Standard Test Methods for Chemical 
 Oxygen Demand ( Dichromate Oxygen Demand) of Water

Test Method B- Micro COD by Sealed Digestion and 
 Spectrometry

This document outlines the 
 testing procedures P1, which must be performed on a monthly 
 basis as indicated by M1 in the above title block, and according to the 
 Directives of the Central Chemical Laboratories.

This test method is 
 essentially equivalent to Test Method A, but it utilize micro volumes of the 
 same reagents contained in a sealable ampule or a screw-top culture tube and a 
 spectrophotometer to measure absorbance or transmittance at selected 
 wavelengths. This test method is applicable where only small sample volumes 
 are available and where large numbers of samples need to be analyzed.

This test method is requires 
 less space per analysis and uses less of the reagents, minimizing costs and 
 volume of wastes discharged.

The dichromate 
reagent and silver catalyst used in this test method are similar to those used 
in Test Method A, but the 
volumes employed are1/20th of those in Test Method A.

A sample 
aliquot is introduced carefully into an
 ampule or a screw-top culture 
tube so that the sample is layered on the top of 
previously introduced reagents and remains there until the ampule or tube 
is sealed. This technique limits evolution of 
heat of solution until the container is sealed, minimizing the loss of volatile organics.

After sealing, the ampule or 
tube is heated in an oven, sand bath,or heated block at 150 2C 
for 2 h. The COD concentration is determined 
spectrophotometrically after digestion. In the low COD range(5 to approximately 50 mg/L), the loss 
of hexavalent chromium is measured at 420 nm, while for the high range (50 to approximately 800 mg/L), 
the increase in trivalent chromium is measured at 600 nm. The ampule or tube serves as the absorption 
cell.

This test method is used to chemically determine 
the maximum quantity of oxygen that could be consumed by biological or natural 
chemical processes due to impurities in water. typically this measurement is 
used to monitor and control oxygen-consuming pollutants, both inorganic and 
organic, in domestic and industrial wastewaters.

Oxygen 
Demand-The amount of oxygen required under specified test conditions for 
the oxidation of waterborne 
organic and inorganic matter.

Interferences 
identified in the test method A are also applicable to the micro procedure. Volatile materials 
will be lost if the sample is mixed with the reagents before the ampule or tube 
is sealed. Volatile materials will also be lost during sample homogenization.

Potentially, the loss 
of volatile organics in the micro procedure will be less than that which 
occur in Test Method A. Thus, 
results between the two methods may differ if volatile materials are involved.

Spectrophotometric 
interferences may exist due to turbidity of precipitated salts that are too 
colloidal to settle in a reasonable 
period of time.

Collect the sample in accordance with Practices D 
3370-76.

Preserve samples by cooling to 4C if analyzed 
within 24 h after sampling, or preserve for up to 28 days at 4C and at pH < 2 by addition of concentrated sulfuric 
acid. The addition of 2 ml of concentrated sulfuric acid per litre at the time of collection will generally 
achieve this requirement. The actual holding time possible without significant change in the COD may be less than 28 
days, especially when easily oxidizable substances are present.

Dissolve 22 g of silver sulfate (Ag2SO4) 
 in a 4.09 Kg (9 Ib) bottle of concentrated sulfuric acid.

Dilute 400 ml of 0.25 N ferrous ammonium sulfate solution,{

acid ( sp gr 1.84), cool and dilute to1 
L}. Standardize against 0.25 N potassium dichromate K2Cr2O7.

solution ( K2Cr2O7) 
to about 250 ml. Add 20 ml of sulfuric acid ( sp gr 1.84) and allow the 
solution to cool. Titrate with the ferrous ammonium sulfate solution
to be standardized, using the phenanthroline 
ferrous sulfate indicator.

N = normality of the ferrous

 dichromate solution, and

Dilute 40 ml of 0.25 N ferrous ammonium 
sulfate solution to 1 L. Standardize against 0.025 N of potassium 
dichromate solution.

Dissolve 1.48 g of 1,10-(ortho)-phenanthroline 
 monohydrate, together with 0.70 g of ferrous sulfate (FeSO4.7H2O), 
 in 100 ml of water. This indicator may be purchased already prepared. If 
 desired, the indicator may be diluted 1:5 for use in this test method.

High Range- Add 10.216 g of
 potassium dichromate, (K2Cr2O7) 
 dried at 103C for 2 h, 167 ml of 
 concentrated sulfuric acid ( sp gr 1.84) 
 and 33.3 g of Mercuric Sulfate ( HgSO4 
 ) to about 750 ml of water, mix, and let cool. Dilute the solution to 1 
 L with water and mix thoroughly.

Low 
 Range- Add 1.022 g of potassium 
 dichromate, (K2Cr2O7) 
 dried at 103C for 2 h,167 ml of 
 concentrated sulfuric acid ( sp gr 1.84) 
 and 33.3 g of Mercuric Sulfate ( HgSO4 
 ) to about 750 ml of water, mix, and let cool. Dilute the solution to 1

Potassium Acid Phthalate Solution Standard (1ml = 
 1mg COD)

High Range- Dilute the following volumes 
 of COD standard solution to 50 ml with water.The high range procedure may be 
 used for COD determination as low as 25 mg/L at the discretion of the analyst.

Low 
Range- Dilute the following volumes of 
potassium acid phthalate standard solution to 200 ml with water. 
At the discretion of the analyst, the upper limit range extended to 
approximately 150 mg/L.

Use the next procedure for the determination of absorbance 
of each standard and blank for high COD range, and low COD.

Prepare calibration curves for each range by plot the absorbance 
of each standard on the abscissa and gm/L of COD on the ordinate. For the low 
procedure, the correlation will have a negative slope; while for high range 
procedure, the slope is positive.

Place 1.5 ml of digestion solution for the 
high range procedure or for low range procedure in a culture tube or glass 
ampule. 
Note 1- Accurate addition of the digestion volume in the low range 
procedure is important because the loss of hexavalent chromium is measured.

Add 3.5 ml of silver sulfate catalyst solution, 
mix, and allow to cool. If the mixed reagents are to be store the sealed or 
capped solution in the dark.

Carefully add 2.5 ml of the sample, standar or 
blank down the side of the tube or ampule so that a layer is formed on top of 
the reagent. Cap the tubes or seal ampules.

Mix the sealed ampules or tube thoroughly. It 
is feasible to mix tubes by holding the tube by the cap and shaking vigorously. 
Complete integrity of the TFE flow-carbon liner in the screw cap is imperative. 
The ampule tube will become hot because of heat of solution.

After mixing, place the ampules or tubes in an oven 
or heating device at 150
 2C 
for 2 h.

Allow the ampules or tubes to cool at room 
temperature. After about 5 min, mix the contents of the ampule or tube 
thoroughly ( to mix condensed water into the solution). Thereafter, permit the 
solution to cool and permit precipitated solids to settle (normally about 30 
min). Rapid cooling will generate colloidal precipitates that are difficult to 
settle.

Make spectrophotometric readings using the 
absorption cells.

Measure the absorbance of the low range solutions 
at 420 nm and the high range solutions at 600 nm.
